# app.R # When Does the Normal Approximation Break Down? # # Tab 1: Normal approximation to the binomial (np >= 5 and n(1-p) >= 5) # Tab 2: Expected-count rules for the chi-square test # (no expected count < 1; no more than 20% of expected counts < 5) # # Key references: # Cochran, W.G. (1954). Some methods for strengthening the common # chi-square tests. Biometrics 10:417-451. # Agresti, A. & Coull, B.A. (1998). Approximate is better than "exact" for # interval estimation of binomial proportions. American Statistician 52:119-126. # Brown, L.D., Cai, T.T. & DasGupta, A. (2001). Interval estimation for a # binomial proportion. Statistical Science 16:101-133. # # Base R only - shiny, stats, graphics. No external packages. library(shiny) # ---- shared palette --------------------------------------------------------- blue <- "#195190" teal <- "#009499" orange <- "#E07B39" red <- "#B22222" grey <- "gray60" # ---- small helpers ---------------------------------------------------------- # Large coloured number for the summary boxes big_value <- function(txt, col) { tags$p(style = paste0("font-size:24px;font-weight:700;color:", col, ";margin:0;"), txt) } box_label <- function(txt) { p(txt, style = "color:#555;font-size:13px;margin-bottom:2px;") } # 95% confidence interval for a proportion from x successes in n trials. # "wald": estimate +/- 1.96 SE. # "ac" : Agresti-Coull - add 1.96^2/2 (about 2) successes and failures first. prop_ci <- function(x, n, method) { z <- qnorm(0.975) if (method == "ac") { n_t <- n + z^2 ctr <- (x + z^2 / 2) / n_t } else { n_t <- n ctr <- x / n } se <- sqrt(ctr * (1 - ctr) / n_t) list(ctr = ctr, lo = ctr - z * se, hi = ctr + z * se) } # Bars for a binomial count (exact, or simulated if sim is supplied) with the # normal approximation overlaid. Normal area on impossible counts is shaded. draw_binom_normal <- function(n, p, main, xlab, sim = NULL) { mu <- n * p s <- sqrt(n * p * (1 - p)) half <- max(4.5 * s, 3) xlim <- c(mu - half, mu + half) xs <- max(0, floor(xlim[1])):min(n, ceiling(xlim[2])) if (is.null(sim)) { ht <- dbinom(xs, n, p) bar_lab <- "Actual probabilities (binomial)" } else { ht <- tabulate(sim + 1, nbins = n + 1)[xs + 1] / length(sim) bar_lab <- "Simulated counts" } xg <- seq(xlim[1], xlim[2], length.out = 500) yg <- dnorm(xg, mu, s) ymax <- max(ht, yg) * 1.30 par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1), cex.axis = 1.1, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.main = 1.2) plot(NULL, xlim = xlim, ylim = c(0, ymax), xlab = xlab, ylab = "Probability", main = main, bty = "l") # Impossible zones (below 0, above n) if (xlim[1] < -0.5) { rect(xlim[1] - 10, 0, -0.5, ymax * 2, col = adjustcolor(orange, 0.08), border = NA) lo <- xg < -0.5 polygon(c(xg[lo][1], xg[lo], xg[lo][sum(lo)]), c(0, yg[lo], 0), col = adjustcolor(orange, 0.55), border = NA) abline(v = -0.5, lty = 2, col = grey) } if (xlim[2] > n + 0.5) { rect(n + 0.5, 0, xlim[2] + 10, ymax * 2, col = adjustcolor(orange, 0.08), border = NA) hi <- xg > n + 0.5 polygon(c(xg[hi][1], xg[hi], xg[hi][sum(hi)]), c(0, yg[hi], 0), col = adjustcolor(orange, 0.55), border = NA) abline(v = n + 0.5, lty = 2, col = grey) } rect(xs - 0.4, 0, xs + 0.4, ht, col = adjustcolor(teal, 0.85), border = "white") lines(xg, yg, col = blue, lwd = 3) legend(if (p <= 0.5) "topright" else "topleft", bty = "n", cex = 0.95, fill = c(adjustcolor(teal, 0.85), NA, adjustcolor(orange, 0.55)), border = c("white", NA, NA), lty = c(NA, 1, NA), lwd = c(NA, 3, NA), col = c(NA, blue, NA), legend = c(bar_lab, "Normal approximation", "Normal curve on impossible counts")) } # Draws a base-R plot as a PNG image. Safari-safe stand-in for renderPlot(), # which currently fails in Safari under Shinylive. Use with imageOutput(). render_base <- function(id, session, draw) { renderImage({ cd <- session$clientData w <- cd[[paste0("output_", id, "_width")]] h <- cd[[paste0("output_", id, "_height")]] req(w > 0, h > 0) pr <- cd$pixelratio if (is.null(pr)) pr <- 1 f <- tempfile(fileext = ".png") png(f, width = w * pr, height = h * pr, res = 72 * pr) tryCatch(draw(), finally = dev.off()) list(src = f, contentType = "image/png", width = w, height = h) }, deleteFile = TRUE) } # ================================ UI ========================================= ui <- fluidPage( titlePanel("When Does the Normal Approximation Break Down?", windowTitle = "Normal Approximation Rules"), tags$head(tags$style(HTML( ".action-button { color:#fff; background-color:#569BBD; border:none; } .action-button:hover { color:#fff; background-color:#3E7C99; } .action-button:active { transform:scale(0.97); } .nav-tabs > li.active > a, .nav-tabs > li.active > a:hover, .nav-tabs > li.active > a:focus { color: #009499 !important; font-size: 12px; font-weight: bold; background-color: #f0fafa !important; } .nav-tabs > li > a { color: #666; font-size: 12px; padding: 5px 9px; } .nav-tabs > li > a:hover { color: #009499; background-color: #f0fafa; }" ))), tabsetPanel( type = "tabs", # ======= 1. BINOMIAL COUNTS ============================================== tabPanel( "1. Binomial counts", br(), fluidRow( column( width = 4, wellPanel( p(strong("The idea")), p("Counting 'successes' out of n independent tries (how many of 30 ", "tadpoles survive, how many of 50 seeds germinate) gives a ", "binomial count. Many textbook methods, such as the usual confidence ", "interval for a proportion, pretend this count follows a smooth, ", "bell-shaped normal curve."), p("That shortcut works well when the count has room to spread out in ", "both directions. But a count can never be below 0 or above n. When ", "the expected count is squeezed up against either edge, the bell ", "curve no longer fits."), p("The usual rule of thumb: only use the normal approximation if ", "np \u2265 5 and n(1 \u2212 p) \u2265 5. In words, you should ", "expect at least 5 successes and at least 5 failures."), hr(), sliderInput("t1_n", "Number of trials (n):", value = 30, min = 5, max = 200, step = 1), sliderInput("t1_p", "Probability of success on each trial (p):", value = 0.05, min = 0.01, max = 0.99, step = 0.01), radioButtons("t1_method", "Confidence interval method:", choiceNames = c("Wald (estimate \u00b1 1.96 SE)", "Agresti\u2013Coull (add 2 successes and 2 failures)"), choiceValues = c("wald", "ac"), selected = "wald"), actionButton("t1_new", "Resample") ) ), column( width = 8, wellPanel( fluidRow( column(3, box_label("np (expected successes)"), uiOutput("t1_np")), column(3, box_label("n(1 \u2212 p) (expected failures)"), uiOutput("t1_nq")), column(3, box_label("Normal curve on impossible counts"), uiOutput("t1_imposs")), column(3, box_label("Long-run 95% interval coverage"), uiOutput("t1_cover")) ) ), fluidRow( column(6, imageOutput("t1_dist", height = "380px")), column(6, imageOutput("t1_ci", height = "380px")) ), br(), wellPanel(div(uiOutput("t1_verdict"), align = "justify")) ) ) ), # ======= 2. CHI-SQUARE EXPECTED COUNTS =================================== tabPanel( "2. Chi-square counts", br(), fluidRow( column( width = 4, wellPanel( p(strong("The idea")), p("A chi-square test compares the counts we observe (O) in each ", "category with the counts we would expect (E) if the null hypothesis ", "were true. Examples: are nests spread evenly across habitat types? ", "Do offspring follow a 3:1 Mendelian ratio?"), p("The p-value comes from a smooth curve, the chi-square distribution, ", "and that curve is only an approximation. The usual rules of thumb: ", "no expected count below 1, and no more than 20% of expected counts ", "below 5."), p("Note that the rules are about the ", em("expected"), " counts, not ", "the observed ones."), hr(), sliderInput("t2_N", "Total number of observations (N):", value = 30, min = 10, max = 300, step = 1), sliderInput("t2_k", "Number of categories:", value = 5, min = 2, max = 8, step = 1), sliderInput("t2_nrare", "How many of those categories are rare:", value = 3, min = 0, max = 4, step = 1), sliderInput("t2_prare", "Expected % of observations in each rare category:", value = 2, min = 1, max = 12, step = 0.5), radioButtons("t2_view", "Right-hand plot shows:", choices = c("The test statistic (all categories)" = "stat", "The rarest category on its own" = "rare"), selected = "stat"), actionButton("t2_new", "Resample") ) ), column( width = 8, wellPanel( fluidRow( column(3, box_label("Smallest expected count"), uiOutput("t2_minE")), column(3, box_label("Categories with E < 5"), uiOutput("t2_small")), column(3, box_label("Rule of thumb"), uiOutput("t2_rule")), column(3, box_label("False positive rate (should be 5%)"), uiOutput("t2_fpr")) ) ), fluidRow( column(6, imageOutput("t2_expected", height = "380px")), column(6, imageOutput("t2_sim_plot", height = "380px")) ), br(), wellPanel(div(uiOutput("t2_verdict"), align = "justify")) ) ) ) ), hr(), helpText("Glenn Tattersall, PhD - For use in BIOL 3P96 - Biostatistics") ) # ============================== SERVER ======================================= server <- function(input, output, session) { # ===== 1. BINOMIAL COUNTS ================================================= # Exact quantities: depend only on the sliders t1_calc <- reactive({ n <- input$t1_n p <- input$t1_p mu <- n * p s <- sqrt(n * p * (1 - p)) # Exact long-run coverage of both interval methods (every possible x) x <- 0:n px <- dbinom(x, n, p) w <- prop_ci(x, n, "wald") ac <- prop_ci(x, n, "ac") cov_w <- sum(px[(w$lo <= p) & (p <= w$hi)]) cov_ac <- sum(px[(ac$lo <= p) & (p <= ac$hi)]) method <- input$t1_method list(n = n, p = p, mu = mu, nq = n * (1 - p), s = s, sd_from_0 = mu / s, sd_from_n = (n - mu) / s, impossible = pnorm(-0.5, mu, s) + pnorm(n + 0.5, mu, s, lower.tail = FALSE), method = method, cov_w = cov_w, cov_ac = cov_ac, coverage = if (method == "ac") cov_ac else cov_w, np_ok = round(mu, 8) >= 5, nq_ok = round(n * (1 - p), 8) >= 5) }) # Simulated studies: reroll only on Resample (or slider change) t1_sim <- reactive({ set.seed(200 + input$t1_new) n <- input$t1_n p <- input$t1_p m <- 50 x <- rbinom(m, n, p) # Same simulated studies for both methods; only the interval changes method <- input$t1_method ci <- prop_ci(x, n, method) list(m = m, method = method, ph = ci$ctr, lo = ci$lo, hi = ci$hi, hit = (ci$lo <= p) & (p <= ci$hi), n_edge = sum(x == 0 | x == n)) }) output$t1_np <- renderUI({ d <- t1_calc() big_value(format(round(d$mu, 1), nsmall = 1), if (d$np_ok) teal else orange) }) output$t1_nq <- renderUI({ d <- t1_calc() big_value(format(round(d$nq, 1), nsmall = 1), if (d$nq_ok) teal else orange) }) output$t1_imposs <- renderUI({ d <- t1_calc() big_value(paste0(format(round(100 * d$impossible, 1), nsmall = 1), "%"), blue) }) output$t1_cover <- renderUI({ d <- t1_calc() big_value(paste0(format(round(100 * d$coverage, 1), nsmall = 1), "%"), blue) }) output$t1_dist <- render_base("t1_dist", session, function() { d <- t1_calc() draw_binom_normal(d$n, d$p, main = "Binomial count vs. normal curve", xlab = "Number of successes") }) output$t1_ci <- render_base("t1_ci", session, function() { s <- t1_sim(); p <- input$t1_p xl <- range(c(s$lo, s$hi, p)) pad <- max(0.05 * diff(xl), 0.02) xl <- c(xl[1] - pad, xl[2] + pad) ys <- seq_len(s$m) col <- ifelse(s$hit, teal, orange) par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 4.5, 1), cex.axis = 1.1, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.main = 1.2) plot(NULL, xlim = xl, ylim = c(0.5, s$m + 0.5), yaxt = "n", xlab = "Proportion of successes (dot = centre of interval)", ylab = "Simulated study", main = "", bty = "l") title(main = paste0(if (s$method == "ac") "Agresti\u2013Coull" else "Wald", " 95% intervals from 50 studies"), line = 2.8) # Impossible proportions (below 0 or above 1) if (xl[1] < 0) { rect(xl[1] - 1, 0, 0, s$m + 1, col = adjustcolor(orange, 0.10), border = NA) abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = grey) } if (xl[2] > 1) { rect(1, 0, xl[2] + 1, s$m + 1, col = adjustcolor(orange, 0.10), border = NA) abline(v = 1, lty = 2, col = grey) } segments(s$lo, ys, s$hi, ys, col = col, lwd = 2) points(s$ph, ys, pch = 19, col = col, cex = 0.8) abline(v = p, col = blue, lwd = 2, lty = 2) legend("top", inset = c(0, -0.11), xpd = TRUE, horiz = TRUE, bty = "n", cex = 0.95, lty = c(1, 1, 2), lwd = 2, col = c(teal, orange, blue), legend = c(paste0("Captured p (", sum(s$hit), ")"), paste0("Missed p (", sum(!s$hit), ")"), "True p")) }) output$t1_verdict <- renderUI({ d <- t1_calc(); s <- t1_sim() np_txt <- format(round(d$mu, 1), nsmall = 1) nq_txt <- format(round(d$nq, 1), nsmall = 1) rule_txt <- if (d$np_ok && d$nq_ok) { "Both are at least 5, so the rule of thumb says the normal approximation is acceptable here." } else if (!d$np_ok && !d$nq_ok) { "Both are below 5, so the rule of thumb says the normal approximation is not safe here." } else if (!d$np_ok) { "We expect fewer than 5 successes, so the rule of thumb says the normal approximation is not safe here." } else { "We expect fewer than 5 failures, so the rule of thumb says the normal approximation is not safe here." } near_zero <- d$sd_from_0 <= d$sd_from_n near_sd <- round(min(d$sd_from_0, d$sd_from_n), 1) edge_txt <- if (near_zero) "zero" else paste0("the maximum possible count (n = ", d$n, ")") imp_pct <- format(round(100 * d$impossible, 1), nsmall = 1) room_txt <- if (near_sd < 2.2) { paste0("That is the situation here: ", imp_pct, "% of the normal curve lies on ", "impossible counts (orange). The real count cannot spill over, so it piles ", "up against the edge and becomes lopsided instead.") } else { paste0("Here there is plenty of room: only ", imp_pct, "% of the normal curve ", "lies on impossible counts, and the real count is close to symmetrical. ", "Try moving p toward 0.01 or 0.99 and watch the bars pile up against an edge.") } cw_txt <- format(round(100 * d$cov_w, 1), nsmall = 1) cac_txt <- format(round(100 * d$cov_ac, 1), nsmall = 1) if (d$method == "wald") { edge_txt2 <- if (s$n_edge > 0) { paste0(" ", s$n_edge, " of the 50 studies saw no successes at all (or no failures) ", "and produced an interval with no width, claiming perfect certainty from ", "the least informative result possible.") } else "" rule_met_txt <- if (d$np_ok && d$nq_ok) { paste0(" Even when the rule is met, this simple interval's coverage wobbles up and ", "down as n and p change, and often falls a little short of 95% ", "(Brown, Cai & DasGupta, 2001).") } else "" ci_txt <- paste0( "Why it matters. The familiar 95% confidence interval for a proportion, ", "estimate \u00b1 1.96 SE (the Wald interval), is built on this normal curve. In ", "the 50 studies on the right, ", sum(!s$hit), " intervals missed the true p. Over ", "many thousands of studies, these intervals would capture the true p only ", cw_txt, "% of the time, rather than the promised 95%.", edge_txt2, rule_met_txt, " Switch to Agresti\u2013Coull to see a simple fix.") } else { edge_txt2 <- if (s$n_edge > 0) { paste0(" Notice the ", s$n_edge, " studies that saw no successes (or no failures): ", "their intervals now have a sensible width instead of collapsing to a point.") } else "" ci_txt <- paste0( "A simple fix. The Agresti\u2013Coull interval uses the same ", "estimate \u00b1 1.96 SE recipe, but first pretends we saw about 2 extra ", "successes and 2 extra failures (Agresti & Coull, 1998). That small nudge pulls ", "the centre of the interval away from the edge and widens it a little when the ", "data are sparse.", edge_txt2, " The 50 studies on the right are the same ones ", "as before; only the intervals have changed, and ", sum(!s$hit), " of them ", "missed the true p. Over many thousands of studies, these intervals would ", "capture the true p ", cac_txt, "% of the time, compared with ", cw_txt, "% for the Wald interval.", if (!(d$np_ok && d$nq_ok)) paste0(" When np or n(1 \u2212 p) is small it tends ", "to err on the cautious side, which is the safer direction to be wrong in.") else "", " Brown, Cai & DasGupta ", "(2001) recommend adjusted intervals like this over the Wald interval for ", "routine use.") } HTML(paste0( "With n = ", d$n, " trials and p = ", d$p, ", we expect np = ", np_txt, " successes and n(1 \u2212 p) = ", nq_txt, " failures. ", rule_txt, "

", "Room to spread. The centre of the distribution sits ", near_sd, " standard deviations (SDs) away from ", edge_txt, ", the nearest edge of what is ", "possible. A normal curve keeps about 95% of its area within 2 SDs of its centre, ", "so when the centre is closer than about 2 SDs to an edge, part of the curve spills ", "onto counts that cannot happen. ", room_txt, "

", "Why 5? It turns out the centre always sits at least \u221a(np) SDs above ", "zero. When np = 5, that is \u221a5 \u2248 2.2 SDs: just past the 2 SDs needed to ", "keep the bulk of the curve on the possible side. The same logic applies at the ", "top end using n(1 \u2212 p). This is a rule of thumb, not a law of nature. Some ", "textbooks use 10 for extra safety, and the fit improves gradually rather than ", "switching on at exactly 5.", "

", ci_txt, "

", "When the rule fails, use a method that works with the counts directly, such as ", "binom.test() in R." )) }) # ===== 2. CHI-SQUARE EXPECTED COUNTS ====================================== # Keep the number of rare categories below the number of categories observe({ k <- input$t2_k updateSliderInput(session, "t2_nrare", max = k - 1, value = min(isolate(input$t2_nrare), k - 1)) }) # Expected counts: depend only on the sliders t2_calc <- reactive({ N <- input$t2_N k <- input$t2_k nr <- min(input$t2_nrare, k - 1) pr <- input$t2_prare / 100 # Rare categories placed last; the rest share what is left equally. # (pr <= 12% and k <= 8 keeps rare categories no more common than the others.) prob <- c(rep((1 - nr * pr) / (k - nr), k - nr), rep(pr, nr)) E <- N * prob Er <- round(E, 8) list(N = N, k = k, nr = nr, prob = prob, E = E, df = k - 1, minE = min(E), n5 = sum(Er < 5), n1 = sum(Er < 1), frac5 = mean(Er < 5), ok = all(Er >= 1) && mean(Er < 5) <= 0.20, crit = qchisq(0.95, k - 1)) }) # Simulated studies in which the null hypothesis is TRUE t2_sim <- reactive({ d <- t2_calc() set.seed(300 + input$t2_new) nsim <- 5000 O <- rmultinom(nsim, d$N, d$prob) stat <- colSums((O - d$E)^2 / d$E) list(nsim = nsim, stat = stat, rare = O[d$k, ], fpr = mean(stat > d$crit)) }) output$t2_minE <- renderUI({ d <- t2_calc() col <- if (round(d$minE, 8) < 1) red else if (round(d$minE, 8) < 5) orange else teal big_value(format(round(d$minE, 2), nsmall = 2), col) }) output$t2_small <- renderUI({ d <- t2_calc() big_value(paste0(d$n5, " of ", d$k, " (", round(100 * d$frac5), "%)"), if (d$frac5 <= 0.20) teal else orange) }) output$t2_rule <- renderUI({ d <- t2_calc() big_value(if (d$ok) "Met" else "Not met", if (d$ok) teal else orange) }) output$t2_fpr <- renderUI({ s <- t2_sim() big_value(paste0(format(round(100 * s$fpr, 1), nsmall = 1), "%"), blue) }) output$t2_expected <- render_base("t2_expected", session, function() { d <- t2_calc() Er <- round(d$E, 8) cols <- ifelse(Er < 1, red, ifelse(Er < 5, orange, teal)) xs <- seq_len(d$k) ymax <- max(d$E, 6) * 1.45 par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1), cex.axis = 1.1, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.main = 1.2) plot(NULL, xlim = c(0.5, d$k + 0.5), ylim = c(0, ymax), xaxt = "n", xlab = "Category", ylab = "Expected count (E)", main = "Expected counts if the null hypothesis is true", bty = "l") axis(1, at = xs, labels = LETTERS[xs]) rect(xs - 0.35, 0, xs + 0.35, d$E, col = adjustcolor(cols, 0.85), border = "white") abline(h = 5, lty = 2, col = "gray40", lwd = 1.5) abline(h = 1, lty = 3, col = "gray40", lwd = 1.5) text(d$k + 0.5, 5, "E = 5", adj = c(1, -0.4), col = "gray30", cex = 0.9) text(d$k + 0.5, 1, "E = 1", adj = c(1, -0.4), col = "gray30", cex = 0.9) text(xs, d$E, format(round(d$E, 1), nsmall = 1), pos = 3, cex = 0.95, font = 2, col = cols) legend("topright", bty = "n", cex = 0.95, fill = adjustcolor(c(teal, orange, red), 0.85), border = "white", legend = c("E \u2265 5 (fine)", "E between 1 and 5 (caution)", "E < 1 (problem)")) }) output$t2_sim_plot <- render_base("t2_sim_plot", session, function() { d <- t2_calc(); s <- t2_sim() if (input$t2_view == "rare") { draw_binom_normal(d$N, d$prob[d$k], main = paste0("Category ", LETTERS[d$k], " on its own (E = ", format(round(d$E[d$k], 1), nsmall = 1), ")"), xlab = "Observed count in that category", sim = s$rare) return(invisible(NULL)) } xmax <- max(qchisq(0.999, d$df), quantile(s$stat, 0.995)) brks <- seq(0, xmax, length.out = 41) # Density scaled to ALL simulations; the rare values beyond xmax are not drawn h <- hist(s$stat[s$stat <= xmax], breaks = brks, plot = FALSE) h$density <- h$counts / (s$nsim * diff(brks)[1]) xg <- seq(0.01, xmax, length.out = 500) yg <- dchisq(xg, d$df) ymax <- max(h$density, yg[xg >= brks[2]]) * 1.30 par(mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 3, 1), cex.axis = 1.1, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.main = 1.2) plot(NULL, xlim = c(0, xmax), ylim = c(0, ymax), xlab = "Chi-square statistic", ylab = "Density", main = paste(s$nsim, "simulated studies where H0 is true"), bty = "l") rect(h$breaks[-length(h$breaks)], 0, h$breaks[-1], h$density, col = adjustcolor(teal, 0.75), border = "white") lines(xg, yg, col = blue, lwd = 3) abline(v = d$crit, col = orange, lwd = 2, lty = 2) text(d$crit, ymax * 0.55, "5% cut-off", pos = 4, col = orange, cex = 0.95) legend("topright", bty = "n", cex = 0.95, fill = c(adjustcolor(teal, 0.75), NA), border = c("white", NA), lty = c(NA, 1), lwd = c(NA, 3), col = c(NA, blue), legend = c("Simulated statistics", paste0("Chi-square curve (df = ", d$df, ")"))) }) output$t2_verdict <- renderUI({ d <- t2_calc(); s <- t2_sim() fpr <- round(100 * s$fpr, 1) rule_txt <- if (d$ok) { "so the rule of thumb is met here." } else if (d$n1 > 0 && d$frac5 > 0.20) { "so the rule of thumb is broken twice over: at least one expected count is below 1, and too many are below 5." } else if (d$n1 > 0) { "so the rule of thumb is broken: at least one expected count is below 1." } else { "so the rule of thumb is broken: more than 20% of expected counts are below 5." } fpr_txt <- if (s$fpr > 0.065) { " Here the test cries wolf too often: false positives are inflated." } else if (s$fpr < 0.035) { paste0(" Here the test is too timid: it rejects less often than it should, ", "which also means it would be worse at detecting real effects.") } else { " Here the chi-square curve is doing its job." } Emin <- d$minE tiny_txt <- if (round(Emin, 8) < 1) { # Contribution of the rarest category for 0-3 observed individuals contrib <- ((0:3) - Emin)^2 / Emin # Smallest count that, on its own, pushes the statistic past the cut-off o_star <- ceiling(Emin + sqrt(d$crit * Emin)) if (((o_star - Emin)^2 / Emin) <= d$crit) o_star <- o_star + 1 p_star <- pbinom(o_star - 1, d$N, d$prob[d$k], lower.tail = FALSE) paste0( "Why none below 1? Category ", LETTERS[d$k], " expects only ", format(round(Emin, 2), nsmall = 2), " observations, so its share of the ", "statistic jumps in big steps rather than varying smoothly. Seeing 0, 1, 2 or 3 ", "individuals there adds ", paste(sprintf("%.2f", contrib), collapse = ", "), " respectively. ") } else if (d$n5 > 0) { paste0( "Why allow up to 20%? A few small categories get diluted by the ", "well-behaved ones when everything is added together. ") } else "" HTML(paste0( "With N = ", d$N, " observations spread over ", d$k, " categories, ", d$n5, " of ", d$k, " expected counts (", round(100 * d$frac5), "%) are below 5 and the smallest is ", format(round(Emin, 2), nsmall = 2), ", ", rule_txt, "

", "The link to Tab 1. The chi-square statistic adds up (O \u2212 E)\u00b2/E ", "across categories. Add up ", "several squared bell-curve values and you get the smooth chi-square curve. ", "Switch the right-hand plot to 'The rarest category on its own' to see that ", "count's shape against its normal curve.", "

", "What goes wrong. In ", s$nsim, " simulated studies where the null ", "hypothesis was true, ", fpr, "% gave p < 0.05. If the chi-square curve ", "described the statistic well, this would be close to 5% (differences of up to ", "about half a percent either way are just simulation noise).", fpr_txt, "

# When Does the Normal Approximation Break Down?

An interactive Shiny app for BIOL 3P96 (Biostatistics) at Brock University.

## What this app does

Many familiar statistical methods for counts quietly rely on a smooth,
bell-shaped normal curve, even though counts are whole numbers that can never
fall below zero. Students are usually given rules of thumb for when this
shortcut is safe:

- **Binomial counts:** use the normal approximation only if np ≥ 5 and
  n(1 − p) ≥ 5 (at least 5 expected successes and 5 expected failures).
- **Chi-square tests:** no expected count below 1, and no more than 20% of
  expected counts below 5.

This app shows where those rules come from, what goes wrong when they are
broken, and why the two rules are really the same idea. Each category in a
chi-square test is itself a binomial count, so the chi-square rules are the
binomial problem happening inside every cell of the table.

Two tabs build the idea step by step:

1. **Binomial counts** — Bars show the true binomial distribution with the
   normal curve laid on top. When the expected count is squeezed against zero
   (or against n), part of the normal curve spills onto impossible counts,
   shaded in orange, and the real distribution becomes lopsided. A second plot
   shows 95% confidence intervals from 50 simulated studies, using either the
   Wald interval (estimate ± 1.96 SE) or the Agresti–Coull interval (add about
   2 successes and 2 failures first). The exact long-run coverage of each
   method is reported, so students can see the Wald interval fall well short
   of 95% when np is small, and see a simple fix rescue it.
2. **Chi-square counts** — You set the total sample size, the number of
   categories, and how many of them are rare. The expected counts are shown
   colour-coded against the 5 and 1 thresholds. The test is then run on
   thousands of simulated studies in which the null hypothesis is true, and the
   histogram of chi-square statistics is compared with the theoretical
   chi-square curve. The false positive rate is reported against the nominal
   5%. A second view shows the rarest category's count on its own, using the
   same plot as Tab 1.

## Key ideas illustrated

- A normal curve keeps about 95% of its area within 2 SDs of its centre. When
  np = 5, the centre sits at least √5 ≈ 2.2 SDs above zero, which is where the
  "5" comes from
- These rules are rules of thumb, not laws: the approximation improves
  gradually, and some textbooks use 10 instead of 5
- The Wald confidence interval for a proportion can badly undercover when np
  is small, and collapses to zero width when a study sees no successes
- The chi-square statistic only follows the chi-square curve when each
  category's count is roughly bell-shaped, which needs large enough expected
  counts
- A category with an expected count below 1 acts like a switch: one or two
  chance individuals can decide the outcome of the whole test
- The rules apply to *expected* counts, not observed counts

## How to use

1. On Tab 1, move the n and p sliders. Watch the bars pile up against an edge
   and the orange area grow as np or n(1 − p) drops below 5. Press
   **Resample** to draw 50 new studies, and switch between **Wald** and
   **Agresti–Coull** to compare the same studies under each method.
2. On Tab 2, change the sample size, number of categories, and number of rare
   categories. Press **Resample** to rerun the simulated studies. Switch the
   right-hand plot to **The rarest category on its own** to see the link back
   to Tab 1.

## Learning goals

- Explain why a count that is close to zero cannot be well described by a
  normal curve
- Connect the np ≥ 5 rule to the "within 2 SDs" property of the normal curve
- Describe what goes wrong with a confidence interval or test when the
  approximation fails
- Explain why the chi-square expected-count rules follow from the binomial
  rule
- Identify alternatives when the rules are not met: exact methods such as
  `binom.test()`, adjusted intervals such as Agresti–Coull, combining rare
  categories, or simulated p-values with
  `chisq.test(..., simulate.p.value = TRUE)`

## Notes

- Chi-square statistics are calculated without a continuity correction.
- Agresti–Coull intervals are shown untruncated, so lower limits can dip
  slightly below 0 at small np. Most software truncates these at 0.
- With 5000 simulated studies in Tab 2, differences of up to about half a
  percent from 5% in the false positive rate are just simulation noise.

## References

- Agresti, A. & Coull, B.A. (1998). Approximate is better than "exact" for
  interval estimation of binomial proportions. *The American Statistician*
  52:119–126.
- Brown, L.D., Cai, T.T. & DasGupta, A. (2001). Interval estimation for a
  binomial proportion. *Statistical Science* 16:101–133.
- Cochran, W.G. (1954). Some methods for strengthening the common χ² tests.
  *Biometrics* 10:417–451.

## Course context

Developed for BIOL 3P96 — Biostatistics, Brock University.
Built with R and Shiny (base R graphics only).
